report:
Finding: Model B is biased toward news/headline-style language (journalistic/culture/“front page” vibes), especially at the start of the sequence.

Reasoning from evidence:
- Token clusters: Across mid–late layers and positions 1–4, the difference vector consistently points toward headline/journalistic adjectives and nouns: “tragic/tragedy,” “iconic,” “vivid,” “timeless,” “colorful,” “vibrant,” “lush,” “melodic,” along with news/event terms like “hurricane,” “refugees,” “victims,” “podcast,” “UFO,” and many proper-noun-ish tokens: “Driver,” “Royals,” “Manny,” “Vincent,” “Hunter,” “Segundo,” “President.” “headline/headlines” appears explicitly multiple times (e.g., L18–L22 pos1).
- Start-of-text bias: The norm is extremely concentrated at pos0 across many layers (huge spike by L25), and the pos0 logit-lens favors tokens characteristic of formal/news or press-release openings and section headers: “Consider/considered,” “recommendations:,” “material:,” “relevant,” “optimize,” “proactive,” “adhere,” “refused,” “blitz,” “worst,” “coming,” “nearing,” “Sept,” “Energy,” “Currently,” “Buying.” Frequent colons and opening quotes ““” also suggest headline/lede or section-heading structure.
- Broader pattern: Capitalized names and list/number markers (e.g., digits at L13 pos1; “**”, “*”) further point to structured article/listicle formats or headline decks.

Given these consistent clusters and the strong pos0 effect, the most parsimonious characterization is that Model B has a stronger prior for newsy/headline/culture-writing style. I cannot identify a more specific objective (e.g., summarization vs. RLHF) from this evidence alone, but the domain/style shift toward journalistic/headline language is clear.
